common-ion-effect-s1.title: Lead(II) chloride in salt solutions
common-ion-effect-s1.text: A student measures the molar solubility of PbCl2 (Ksp = 1.7 × 10−5 at 25 °C) in water and in three NaCl solutions at 25 °C. NaCl is a soluble salt that dissociates completely. PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2 Cl−(aq).

common-ion-effect-s2.title: Silver chromate in three liquids
common-ion-effect-s2.text: Red-brown silver chromate, Ag2CrO4, is slightly soluble: Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2 Ag+(aq) + CrO42−(aq), Ksp = 1.1 × 10−12 at 25 °C. A student adds excess solid to three beakers at 25 °C: beaker 1, pure water; beaker 2, 0.050 M AgNO3; beaker 3, 0.050 M K2CrO4. AgNO3 and K2CrO4 are soluble salts.

items.q: What trend does the table show?
options: PbCl<sub>2</sub> is less soluble when more Cl<sup>−</sup> is already in solution.
PbCl<sub>2</sub> is more soluble in salt solutions than in water.
The solubility of PbCl<sub>2</sub> does not depend on [NaCl].
PbCl<sub>2</sub> is less soluble because K<sub>sp</sub> decreases in salt solutions.

why.correct: This is the common-ion effect: an ion already present (Cl⁻ from NaCl) lowers the solubility of a salt that contains it.
options: Right: the solubility falls from 1.6 × 10<sup>−2</sup> M in water to 2.7 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M in 0.25 M NaCl.
The numbers fall, not rise, as [NaCl] increases.
The solubility changes by about a factor of 10 across the table.
The trend is right, but the cause is wrong: K<sub>sp</sub> is the same in every solution at 25 °C.

items.q: Which explanation of the trend would earn credit?
options: Cl<sup>−</sup> from NaCl raises Q, so less PbCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves before Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
NaCl lowers K<sub>sp</sub> for PbCl<sub>2</sub>.
Na<sup>+</sup> ions react with Pb<sup>2+</sup> and remove it.
NaCl takes up the water, leaving less for PbCl<sub>2</sub> to dissolve in.

why.correct: Reason with Q and K<sub>sp</sub>: Cl⁻ from NaCl raises Q, so the equilibrium sits further toward the solid and less PbCl₂ dissolves.
options: Right: with Cl⁻ already present, a smaller [Pb²⁺] is enough to make Q reach K<sub>sp</sub>.
K<sub>sp</sub> depends only on temperature; the common ion changes Q.
Na⁺ is a spectator ion here. The shared ion, Cl⁻, is what matters.
The solutions are dilute; the effect is an equilibrium effect of Cl⁻, not a shortage of water.

items.q: Using the small-x approximation ([Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.25 M), calculate the molar solubility of PbCl<sub>2</sub> in 0.25 M NaCl.

mistakes.why: Value: [Cl⁻] is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>: s = K<sub>sp</sub> / (0.25)².
Value: that is the solubility in pure water. Include the 0.25 M Cl⁻ from NaCl.
Value: in this solution [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.25 M, not 2s, so do not multiply by 4.

items.q: A student uses the small-x approximation for 0.010 M NaCl and gets s = 1.7 × 10<sup>−1</sup> M. What went wrong?
options: 2s is not small next to 0.010 M.
The student forgot to square [Cl<sup>−</sup>].
K<sub>sp</sub> should be multiplied by 4.
Nothing; a smaller [Cl<sup>−</sup>] means a larger solubility.

why.correct: Always check the approximation. Here 2s would be 0.34 M, far more than 5% of 0.010 M; the exact solution (about ${sci(svals[1], 2, { force: true })} M, below the pure-water value) needs the full expression.
options: Right: 2s would be 0.34 M, far more than 0.010 M, so 0.010 + 2s is not ≈ 0.010. A solubility above the pure-water value is a sure sign.
Squaring was done: 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ / (0.010)² = 0.17. The problem is the approximation itself.
The 4 appears only when [Cl⁻] = 2s with no other source of Cl⁻.
A common ion can only lower solubility; 0.17 M is ten times the pure-water value, so something is wrong.

items.q: A saturated solution of PbCl<sub>2</sub> with excess solid is at 25 °C. Solid NaCl is dissolved in it. Predict each quantity after equilibrium is restored.

variables.name: [Pb<sup>2+</sup>]
variables.why: Added Cl⁻ makes Q > K<sub>sp</sub>, so PbCl₂ precipitates, removing Pb²⁺.

variables.name: [Cl<sup>−</sup>]
variables.why: Some added Cl⁻ precipitates, but most stays: the shift only partly counteracts the change.

why.correct: A common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>, so solid forms until Q = K<sub>sp</sub> again; K<sub>sp</sub> itself is unchanged.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 2.

mistakes.why: Value: [Ag⁺] is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>: s = K<sub>sp</sub> / (0.050)².
Value: [Ag⁺] ≈ 0.050 M from AgNO₃; it is not doubled. The 2 in 2s applies only to Ag⁺ coming from the dissolving salt.
Value: that is the solubility in pure water; include the Ag⁺ already present.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 3.

mistakes.why: Value: that is [Ag⁺] = 2s. Divide by 2 to get s.
Value: K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(0.050), so (2s)² = K<sub>sp</sub>/0.050; take a square root.

items.q: Rank the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in the three beakers, from greatest to least.

why.correct: Any common ion lowers solubility. Because [Ag⁺] is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>, adding Ag⁺ cuts the solubility more than adding the same concentration of CrO₄²⁻.
options: Right: 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M in water, 2.3 × 10<sup>−6</sup> M with chromate, 4.4 × 10<sup>−10</sup> M with silver. Ag⁺ is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>, so the silver common ion lowers solubility far more.
Both common ions lower solubility, but Ag⁺ (squared in K<sub>sp</sub>) has the larger effect, so beaker 2 is lowest.
Common ions lower solubility, so water gives the highest value, not the lowest.
K<sub>sp</sub> is the same in all three, but solubility is not.

items.q: How does K<sub>sp</sub> of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 2 compare with its value in beaker 1?
options: It is the same.
It is smaller, because less solid dissolves.
It is larger, because [Ag<sup>+</sup>] is larger.
It is undefined, because Ag<sup>+</sup> comes from two sources.

why.correct: K<sub>sp</sub> changes only with temperature. In beaker 2, [Ag⁺] is high and [CrO₄²⁻] low, but [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] is still 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
options: Right: both are at 25 °C. The common ion changes the solubility, not K<sub>sp</sub>.
Less solid dissolves, but the ion concentrations still multiply to the same K<sub>sp</sub>.
[Ag⁺] is larger and [CrO₄²⁻] is smaller; the product is unchanged.
K<sub>sp</sub> uses the total [Ag⁺], whatever its source.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl is 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. Calculate its molar solubility in 0.020 M CaCl<sub>2</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: each CaCl₂ gives two Cl⁻, so [Cl⁻] = 0.040 M, not 0.020 M.
Value: that is the solubility in pure water. Include the Cl⁻ from CaCl₂.

items.q: By what factor is the solubility of AgCl (K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>) lower in 0.10 M NaCl than in pure water? (Give s<sub>water</sub> / s<sub>NaCl</sub>.)

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the other way. s in water is the larger value.

items.q: Which added solutes would lower the solubility of CaF<sub>2</sub> in water? Select all that apply.
options: NaF
NaCl
KNO<sub>3</sub>
Sugar (C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>)

why.correct: Only an ion that appears in the solubility equilibrium (Ca²⁺ or F⁻) raises Q and lowers the solubility. Of these, only NaF supplies one.
options: Right: it supplies F⁻, a common ion.
Neither Na⁺ nor Cl⁻ is in the CaF₂ equilibrium, so Q is unchanged.
Neither K⁺ nor NO₃⁻ is in the CaF₂ equilibrium.
A nonelectrolyte adds no ions, so it does not change Q.

items.q: A saturated solution of BaSO<sub>4</sub> is at equilibrium with the solid. Concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> solution is added. Which statement gives the best justification of what happens?
options: Q rises above K<sub>sp</sub>, so BaSO<sub>4</sub> precipitates.
K<sub>sp</sub> rises because more sulfate is present, so more BaSO<sub>4</sub> dissolves.
Na<sup>+</sup> replaces Ba<sup>2+</sup> in the solid.
The reverse reaction speeds up, so the system shifts.

why.correct: Adding a common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>; the net reaction is precipitation, which lowers [Ba²⁺] until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
options: Right: claim (precipitate forms), evidence (sulfate added), reasoning (Q > K<sub>sp</sub>).
K<sub>sp</sub> does not change with concentration, and adding a common ion lowers solubility.
Na⁺ is a spectator; the solid stays BaSO₄.
Rate language alone does not earn the point; compare Q with K<sub>sp</sub>.

items.q: Put the steps for calculating solubility in a solution with a common ion in order.
options: Find the concentration of the common ion from the soluble salt (count its ions per formula unit).
Write each ion concentration: s times the coefficient, plus the common-ion concentration for the shared ion.
Approximate (common ion + small term) ≈ common ion, and solve K<sub>sp</sub> for s.
Check that the dropped term is under 5% of the common-ion concentration.

why.correct: The common ion sets one concentration; the small-x approximation from topic 7.7 makes the algebra simple; always check it.

items.q: Why does adding a common ion lower solubility, at the particle level?
options: Ions rejoin the solid more often, so less salt dissolves before the rates match.
The added ions coat the surface of the solid so water does not reach it.
The added ions make the water less polar.
The added ions react with the solid to make a new compound.

why.correct: Precipitation happens when dissolved ions meet the solid. A higher concentration of one of the ions speeds precipitation, so the dissolving and precipitation rates become equal with less salt dissolved.
options: Right: the precipitation rate rises with the ion concentration, so less salt needs to dissolve before the rates match.
Dissolved ions do not coat the solid; the effect comes from the equilibrium.
Dilute ions barely change water as a solvent.
The solid is the same compound; only the balance between dissolving and precipitation changes.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is 5.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup>. Calculate [Mg<sup>2+</sup>] that can remain dissolved in a solution in which [OH<sup>−</sup>] is held at 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M.

mistakes.why: Value: [OH⁻] is given directly as 1.0 × 10⁻³ M; do not double it.
